# Testing builds

The builds every test of [`testing`](../SKILL.md) runs against, and how coverage is measured
over them.

## 1. Builds

Tests run against the target's prebuilt, immutable builds, recorded as the `variants` of
`crustify/artifacts/build.json`: each an out-of-tree `dir` and the `configure` and `build`
commands run from it, its `version` raised whenever a command changes. They are:

- `plain`, the functional baseline;
- `coverage`, the coverage-instrumented build for campaign measurements, instrumented as
  [Coverage](#2-coverage) describes; and
- one variant per sanitizer the campaign enables, whose tests build the Rust with the same
  LLVM sanitizer as the C, the C's clang of the pinned nightly's LLVM major version as for
  coverage, so that one runtime serves both and a report from the Rust's own unsafe code is
  caught too, and whose C consumers that link the safe crate's Rust static library, from a
  module's switch on, link one built with the same instrumentation:
  - `asan-ubsan`, the general build, which FFI and lifecycle tests use;
  - `msan`, which instruments every component, the standard library included;
  - `tsan`, separate from `asan-ubsan`, since ASan and TSan instrument the same memory
    operations and their runtimes conflict; and
  - `bsan`, when BorrowSanitizer's `bsan` toolchain is installed and answers its version;
    it instruments the C through its own matched clang.

A Rust- or bindgen-only change reuses a matching variant: same C revision, `build.json`
version, compiler and instrumentation. Nothing writes into a variant's `dir`: each run's
logs and outputs go to paths of its own. A change to the compiled target, or no matching
variant, needs a private build, which the raw bindings link when `CRUSTIFY_BUILD_DIR` names
it in place of a variant, and the shared variants are rebuilt once that change lands.

## 2. Coverage

Coverage is counted with one instrument for C and Rust, so that a C figure and a Rust
figure, and the campaign's figures and those of a crate it is compared with, are counted
alike, and count the code under test only:

- **Instrumentation.** The `coverage` variant compiles the C with clang's source-based
  coverage, `-fprofile-instr-generate -fcoverage-mapping` in its compile and link flags,
  from a clang of the pinned nightly's LLVM major version, and the Rust is compiled on that
  nightly with `-C instrument-coverage`. One profiling runtime counts both, into a profile
  per process and module (`LLVM_PROFILE_FILE=<dir>/%p-%m.profraw`), and the nightly's
  `llvm-profdata` and `llvm-cov` read both. gcc's coverage instrumentation and gcov are not used: their
  lines follow the line table of the optimized code, which the optimization level changes,
  so their figures cannot be compared with Rust's.
- **Test code.** Test code is not instrumented, so it is neither credited as covered nor
  counted as code to cover. Counted, it would inflate the suite that runs it, whose own
  lines run whenever it does, and deflate every other suite, whose denominator would hold
  lines it never runs. Every test item of the measured crate, under `#[test]`,
  `#[cfg(test)]` or a `cfg` that requires `test`, carries `#[coverage(off)]`, which covers
  everything nested in it, and the crate root enables `#![feature(coverage_attribute)]`.
  The attributes are added in a scratch copy of the measured tree under `crustify/tmp/`,
  which is measured in its place, so that the measured crates are not changed. Integration
  test crates, examples, benches, the crate root's build script and the generated raw
  bindings under `sys/` are left out of the report by path. Test code that is not an item, such as a `#[cfg(test)]`
  block inside a library function, stays instrumented, and is reported with the figures.
- **Objects.** C coverage is read from the objects the tests load: the variant's shared
  libraries, or the object files a crate links statically, every TU compiled into them
  counting, and one no test reaches at zero. A figure covers the sources of the library it
  names, selected by directory, so that the copies of its inline functions and of its TUs
  that other libraries compile, the configuration headers the build generates and the C's
  own tests count toward none. Rust coverage is read from every test and doctest binary of
  the crate. All objects are passed for every suite, so that every suite has the same
  denominator.
- **Suites.** Each suite runs alone, into its own profile directory, merged into one
  profile; the total merges the suites' profiles, so it is their union, never their sum.
  Doctests are a suite of their own.
- **Figures.** The figures are the totals `llvm-cov report` prints, unmodified: line,
  function and region coverage, line coverage leading. Its per-line views (`llvm-cov show`
  and the LCOV export) count lines differently, marking the bodies of C macro definitions
  as executed: they locate gaps, and never compute a figure.
- **Comparisons.** A crate the campaign is compared with is measured the same way: its
  test items marked in a scratch copy, its own release of the C built as the `coverage`
  variant is, its suites run alone, and its figures read from `llvm-cov report`. A
  comparison names its scope, and both sides are measured over the same one.

### 2.1 A worklist's coverage

A worklist's tests run against the campaign's `coverage` variant, measured as
above, and coverage is inspected for the C and Rust execution
paths belonging to the worklist. Focused tests are added to cover its reachable uncovered
paths. Paths that remain uncovered because they are unreachable, environment-dependent, or
intentionally nondeterministic are reported as such.

Coverage is maximized, not gated. Each worklist reports its regions and branches beside
its lines, and which of its types' states and transitions, as the analysis lists them, its
tests reach. In a port, a module's C is the reference until its switch: its coverage

against what its own C tests reach. From the switch on, the module's coverage is its

---
name: reviewing-reports
description: "How a review's findings are filed: report directories, classes, evidence, conditions, root causes, notes, reproducers, and disclosure drafts with their upstream check and status. Read before filing or revisiting a finding, drafting or checking a disclosure, or consolidating a campaign's reports."
---

# Reviewing: reports

What a review files for the defects [`reviewing`](../SKILL.md)'s objectives name: a report
per root cause, the reproducer that proves it, and, under `disclose`, the draft its
project's maintainers are sent.

## 1. Reports

A review batch files its findings under its reviews dir, as
[`layout`](../../../operations/layout/SKILL.md)'s Reviews section spells it,
each in its own `<slug>` directory, holding its report and, when it has one, its
reproducer, in the sub-directory of its objective:

| objective | sub-directory |
|---|---|
| `unsafety` | `unsafe/` |
| `contracts`, of a gateway | `contracts/ffi_export/` |
| `contracts`, of other unsafe code | `contracts/ffi_import/` |
| `ub`, on the safe interface | `ub_safe/` |
| `ub`, on the unsafe interface | `ub_unsafe/` |
| `ub`, through an export | `ub_export/` |
| `equiv` | `equiv/` |
| `logic` | `logic/` |
| `ergonomics` | `ergonomics/` |
| `idiom` | `idiom/` |
| `conventions` | `conventions/` |
| `misc` | `misc/` |

A tool may add sub-directories for findings on its own output. A defect in a tool
rather than in the reviewed codebase, Crustify included, is no finding: it is a proposal,
with its reproducer, as [`evolution`](../../../crustify/evolution/SKILL.md)'s Proposals
section describes.

A report states what is wrong, where, the evidence that proves it, and, under `fix`, how it
was fixed. It names the tier that caught the finding, and the tiers that had the same code
in scope before it and passed it. The tiers are a batch's own gates, a review batch, a
module pass, a switch, a later stage's review, a revisit, a ship point's gates and a
consumer. A finding caught by a later tier than the first that had it in scope is an
escape. A finding of `ub` or `contracts` also names the pattern of
[`soundness`](../../../rust/soundness/SKILL.md) it is an instance of, or `new`. A finding that a switch, a ship point's gates or a consumer catches is filed by the
review batch it is handed to, which names that tier. It carries everything needed to rerun
its reproducer from a clean checkout: the exact command and the sanitizer output or failing
assertion it produced. Neither a report nor a reproducer carries an API key, in a core dump
or anywhere else: a reviews dir may be published.

### 1.1 Header

A report opens with its header, one `key: value` line each:

- `class`, as [Classes](#12-classes) gives it;
- `evidence`: what decided it, a sanitizer, Miri or a failing assertion, by name. A
  result that only an aliasing model reports, Stacked Borrows, Tree Borrows or BSan, adds
  `aliasing-model only`; one that rests on a claim the Rust Reference does not settle,
  such as a reference to an uninhabited opaque type or to a partly initialised struct,
  adds `unsettled`. Either says so wherever the report or its disclosure states the
  defect, and neither is called undefined behaviour without that qualifier;
- `conditions`: the Cargo features, target and `cfg`s it needs, whether it needs a system
  C library rather than the bundled one, or a version of it, and the revisions it
  reproduces on; and
- `same-cause`, where another report in the tree has the same root cause: that report's
  dir.

### 1.2 Classes

| class | what the report shows |
|---|---|
| `soundness` | undefined behaviour reached from the safe public API, from the unsafe public API within its `# Safety` obligations, or by C through an export within the C declaration's contract |
| `c-bug` | a defect of the C library itself, which its own API reaches without the crate's doing |
| `behaviour` | no undefined behaviour: a panic, a wrong value, a swallowed error, a leak, or a divergence from the C or the specification |
| `nit` | nothing a consumer can observe: a missing or imprecise `// SAFETY:` justification, an under-documented `# Safety` obligation that no reproducer breaks, or an API-shape finding of `unsafety`, `ergonomics`, `idiom` or `conventions` |

What only misuse can reach is not reportable and gets no report: a private item no public
API reaches with the inputs in question, or an `unsafe` API called against its stated
obligations.

### 1.3 Root causes

A report is one root cause. Sites that share a defect are one report that lists them,
whatever objective or instrument met each. Before a finding is filed, the reports already
in the tree are searched for its cause, by site and mechanism, not by name: one a batch
of its own filed takes the new site; one another batch filed is named in `same-cause`.

### 1.4 Notes

Outside a Crustify-generated crate, a `nit` gets no report directory: it is one line, with
its site, in the batch's `notes.md` at the root of its reviews dir, grouped by kind, such
as unjustified `unsafe` blocks. So is a candidate that reading supports and no true
reproducer can show, as `unproven`, with why none is possible. A campaign keeps one such
note per crate, merged from its batches'.

## 2. Reproducers

A `ub`, `equiv` or `logic` candidate becomes a finding only once a reproducer proves it,
and so does a `contracts` candidate that claims a contract can be broken. A contract that
merely asks for more than the implementation needs, or a missing justification, is a
finding without one.

- A UB reproducer triggers one of the available sanitizers from Rust, and its report
  carries the sanitizer's trace. One targeting the safe public API carries
  `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`; one targeting the unsafe API, or breaking a contract, honours
  the `# Safety` obligation, and its report says, for each `unsafe` it writes, why the
  defect is still the crate's. One reaching an export calls it as C would, through its
  raw binding, within the C declaration's contract.
- An equivalence reproducer fails one of [`testing`](../../testing/SKILL.md)'s equivalence
  comparisons while running the raw C and the public Rust API, and its report carries the
  failing assertion. Once the C is gone, a behaviour finding is a `logic` one.
- A logic reproducer fails a Rust assertion of what the specification it cites requires,
  and its report carries the failing assertion.

Each reproducer is a standalone Cargo package: its `Cargo.toml` declares an empty
`[workspace]` table and depends on the affected crate through a relative `path`, and its
`src/main.rs` runs one scenario, so that running it exits non-zero on the affected commit.

Whatever its kind, a reproducer is a true proof of concept:

- it links the affected crate itself and reaches the defect through its public API: it
  copies none of the crate's code, a private module included, and stands in for no part
  of the crate or of the C with a stub or a model;
- it is deterministic: every run gives the same verdict, and one that depends on an
  interleaving runs under the sanitizer that reports the race whichever thread wins;
- it fails visibly, for the reason its report states, and would pass were the defect
  absent: a comparison that passes, or a failure of the reproducer's own setup, proves
  nothing; and
- it is minimal: one scenario, with nothing the failure does not need.

## 3. Disclosure

Under `disclose`, a report of class `soundness`, `c-bug` or `behaviour` gets a
`disclosure.md` beside it, a `c-bug`'s addressed to the C library's project. It is a draft
for the user to send: a review opens no issue, pull request or advisory, and sends and
posts nothing.

### 3.1 Upstream check

Before a draft is written, the project is checked upstream, unless the campaign's
settings turn the check off: its tracker's open and closed issues and pull requests are
searched for the defect, and the reproducer is rerun on the latest release and on the tip
of the default branch, not only on the reviewed revision. A query to an outside service
carries only generic technical terms, an API's name or an error's text, never the
report, the reproducer or anything of the campaign or its user. A defect already reported
or already fixed gets no draft beyond its header, with the issue or the fix as its
status, and its report's `conditions` say which of the revisions are affected. Without
the check, the header says `upstream: unchecked`.

### 3.2 Draft

`disclosure.md` opens with a header, then a `---` line, then the body the user sends:

- `status`: `to file`; `DO NOT FILE: <reason>`; `REPORTED: <url>`, the upstream issue; or
  `FIXED: <url>`, the pull request or commit that fixed it. It is the one record of the
  disclosure's fate, kept current as the user reports what they sent;
- `channel`: where the project asks for such reports, from its `SECURITY.md`, its issue
  templates and its contributing guide at the default branch: a private advisory or an
  email, with the maintainers named, or a public issue. A project that refuses
  machine-written text is flagged here, and its draft is notes for the user to rewrite,
  not text to paste; and
- `title`: a plain line naming the API and the effect, which the body does not repeat as
  a heading.

The body follows the project's conventions and holds, in 150 to 250 words of prose:

- two to four sentences on what goes wrong, and under which of the report's `conditions`;
- the minimal reproducer inline, and a few lines of its real output;
- the exact versions it was run on, the crate's, the C library's and the toolchain's; and
- one or two sentences on a possible fix.

Every statement in it is one the review verified by running or reading: no history, no
counts, no comparison with other projects and no speculation about exploitability. It
uses none of the campaign's vocabulary, such as a wave, a batch or an objective. It ends
with: `Found by [Crustify](https://github.com/crustify-rs/crustify), an experimental
UB/soundness auditing agent developed at UC Berkeley and running on <model name>, then
manually reviewed and independently reproduced.`

A possible fix may be tried on a copy of the tree in the batch's scratch, without `fix`:
the draft calls it tested only when the reproducer stops failing and the crate's own
tests pass with it. A patch is offered only under `fix`.

description: "The regression gates work lands through, by event: a batch's scoped gates, a wave's, a module's end or switch from C and a ship point's; campaign mode and packaging, sanitizers, BSan and Miri, rebases under the landing lock, and a port batch's export checks. Read before running a batch's gates, landing, integrating a module or shipping."

# Testing gates

The gates every landing passes, over the tests [`testing`](../SKILL.md) classifies and the
builds [`testing-builds`](../builds/SKILL.md) describes.

## 1. Regressions

Every batch checks, formats and lints the workspace on the tree it lands, with warnings
denied, as [`toolchain`](../../../rust/toolchain/SKILL.md) describes, and tests what its
change can affect: its module and the modules that depend on it, as `modules.json` records
them, each by its tests' module paths.

Every build of those gates runs in the raw bindings' campaign mode, as
[`bindgen`](../../../rust/bindgen/SKILL.md)'s Build modes section describes, so that each fails when the
committed bindings do not match their input. A batch that changed the raw bindings, or a
landing that changes `c/`, also packages the safe crate, built alone in bundled mode from
the C it packages, with no build variant selected. Until the out-of-tree wrappers are
published, each crate the package depends on is patched to its local source, so that the
package builds alone.

The tests run against the matching variant, or a private replacement, and each event runs
them to its own depth:

- a batch: the tests above, plain and under ASan/UBSan, and its own tests under each other
  sanitizer its items call for, such as TSan where it asserts `Send` or `Sync` or adds a
  threaded callback, or MSan where C leaves memory it hands over partly unwritten;

# Reviewing: reports

What a review files for the defects [`reviewing`](../SKILL.md)'s objectives name: a report
per root cause, the reproducer that proves it, and, under `disclose`, the draft its
project's maintainers are sent.

## 1. Reports

A review batch files its findings under its reviews dir, as
[`layout`](../../../operations/layout/SKILL.md)'s Reviews section spells it,
each in its own `<slug>` directory, holding its report and, when it has one, its
reproducer, in the sub-directory of its objective:

| objective | sub-directory |
|---|---|
| `unsafety` | `unsafe/` |
| `contracts`, of a gateway | `contracts/ffi_export/` |
| `contracts`, of other unsafe code | `contracts/ffi_import/` |
| `ub`, on the safe interface | `ub_safe/` |
| `ub`, on the unsafe interface | `ub_unsafe/` |
| `ub`, through an export | `ub_export/` |
| `equiv` | `equiv/` |
| `logic` | `logic/` |
| `ergonomics` | `ergonomics/` |
| `idiom` | `idiom/` |
| `conventions` | `conventions/` |
| `misc` | `misc/` |

A tool may add sub-directories for findings on its own output. A defect in a tool
rather than in the reviewed codebase, Crustify included, is no finding: it is a proposal,
with its reproducer, as [`evolution`](../../../crustify/evolution/SKILL.md)'s Proposals
section describes.

A report states what is wrong, where, the evidence that proves it, and, under `fix`, how it
was fixed. It names the tier that caught the finding, and the tiers that had the same code
in scope before it and passed it. The tiers are a batch's own gates, a review batch, a
module pass, a switch, a later stage's review, a revisit, a ship point's gates and a
consumer. A finding caught by a later tier than the first that had it in scope is an
escape. A finding of `ub` or `contracts` also names the pattern of
[`soundness`](../../../rust/soundness/SKILL.md) it is an instance of, or `new`. A finding that a switch, a ship point's gates or a consumer catches is filed by the
review batch it is handed to, which names that tier. It carries everything needed to rerun
its reproducer from a clean checkout: the exact command and the sanitizer output or failing
assertion it produced. Neither a report nor a reproducer carries an API key, in a core dump
or anywhere else: a reviews dir may be published.

### 1.1 Header

A report opens with its header, one `key: value` line each:

- `class`, as [Classes](#12-classes) gives it;
- `evidence`: what decided it, a sanitizer, Miri or a failing assertion, by name. A
  result that only an aliasing model reports, Stacked Borrows, Tree Borrows or BSan, adds
  `aliasing-model only`; one that rests on a claim the Rust Reference does not settle,
  such as a reference to an uninhabited opaque type or to a partly initialised struct,
  adds `unsettled`. Either says so wherever the report or its disclosure states the
  defect, and neither is called undefined behaviour without that qualifier;
- `conditions`: the Cargo features, target and `cfg`s it needs, whether it needs a system
  C library rather than the bundled one, or a version of it, and the revisions it
  reproduces on; and
- `same-cause`, where another report in the tree has the same root cause: that report's
  dir.

### 1.2 Classes

| class | what the report shows |
|---|---|
| `soundness` | undefined behaviour reached from the safe public API, from the unsafe public API within its `# Safety` obligations, or by C through an export within the C declaration's contract |
| `c-bug` | a defect of the C library itself, which its own API reaches without the crate's doing |
| `behaviour` | no undefined behaviour: a panic, a wrong value, a swallowed error, a leak, or a divergence from the C or the specification |
| `nit` | nothing a consumer can observe: a missing or imprecise `// SAFETY:` justification, an under-documented `# Safety` obligation that no reproducer breaks, or an API-shape finding of `unsafety`, `ergonomics`, `idiom` or `conventions` |

What only misuse can reach is not reportable and gets no report: a private item no public
API reaches with the inputs in question, or an `unsafe` API called against its stated
obligations.

### 1.3 Root causes

A report is one root cause. Sites that share a defect are one report that lists them,
whatever objective or instrument met each. Before a finding is filed, the reports already
in the tree are searched for its cause, by site and mechanism, not by name: one a batch
of its own filed takes the new site; one another batch filed is named in `same-cause`.

### 1.4 Notes

Outside a Crustify-generated crate, a `nit` gets no report directory: it is one line, with
its site, in the batch's `notes.md` at the root of its reviews dir, grouped by kind, such
as unjustified `unsafe` blocks. So is a candidate that reading supports and no true
reproducer can show, as `unproven`, with why none is possible. A campaign keeps one such
note per crate, merged from its batches'.

## 2. Reproducers

A `ub`, `equiv` or `logic` candidate becomes a finding only once a reproducer proves it,
and so does a `contracts` candidate that claims a contract can be broken. A contract that
merely asks for more than the implementation needs, or a missing justification, is a
finding without one.

- A UB reproducer triggers one of the available sanitizers from Rust, and its report
  carries the sanitizer's trace. One targeting the safe public API carries
  `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`; one targeting the unsafe API, or breaking a contract, honours
  the `# Safety` obligation, and its report says, for each `unsafe` it writes, why the
  defect is still the crate's. One reaching an export calls it as C would, through its
  raw binding, within the C declaration's contract.
- An equivalence reproducer fails one of [`testing`](../../testing/SKILL.md)'s equivalence
  comparisons while running the raw C and the public Rust API, and its report carries the
  failing assertion. Once the C is gone, a behaviour finding is a `logic` one.
- A logic reproducer fails a Rust assertion of what the specification it cites requires,
  and its report carries the failing assertion.

Each reproducer is a standalone Cargo package: its `Cargo.toml` declares an empty
`[workspace]` table and depends on the affected crate through a relative `path`, and its
`src/main.rs` runs one scenario, so that running it exits non-zero on the affected commit.

Whatever its kind, a reproducer is a true proof of concept:

- it links the affected crate itself and reaches the defect through its public API: it
  copies none of the crate's code, a private module included, and stands in for no part
  of the crate or of the C with a stub or a model;
- it is deterministic: every run gives the same verdict, and one that depends on an
  interleaving runs under the sanitizer that reports the race whichever thread wins;
- it fails visibly, for the reason its report states, and would pass were the defect
  absent: a comparison that passes, or a failure of the reproducer's own setup, proves
  nothing; and
- it is minimal: one scenario, with nothing the failure does not need.

## 3. Disclosure

Under `disclose`, a report of class `soundness`, `c-bug` or `behaviour` gets a
`disclosure.md` beside it, a `c-bug`'s addressed to the C library's project. It is a draft
for the user to send: a review opens no issue, pull request or advisory, and sends and
posts nothing.

### 3.1 Upstream check

Before a draft is written, the project is checked upstream, unless the campaign's
settings turn the check off: its tracker's open and closed issues and pull requests are
searched for the defect, and the reproducer is rerun on the latest release and on the tip
of the default branch, not only on the reviewed revision. A query to an outside service
carries only generic technical terms, an API's name or an error's text, never the
report, the reproducer or anything of the campaign or its user. A defect already reported
or already fixed gets no draft beyond its header, with the issue or the fix as its
status, and its report's `conditions` say which of the revisions are affected. Without
the check, the header says `upstream: unchecked`.

### 3.2 Draft

`disclosure.md` opens with a header, then a `---` line, then the body the user sends:

- `status`: `to file`; `DO NOT FILE: <reason>`; `REPORTED: <url>`, the upstream issue; or
  `FIXED: <url>`, the pull request or commit that fixed it. It is the one record of the
  disclosure's fate, kept current as the user reports what they sent;
- `channel`: where the project asks for such reports, from its `SECURITY.md`, its issue
  templates and its contributing guide at the default branch: a private advisory or an
  email, with the maintainers named, or a public issue. A project that refuses
  machine-written text is flagged here, and its draft is notes for the user to rewrite,
  not text to paste; and
- `title`: a plain line naming the API and the effect, which the body does not repeat as
  a heading.

The body follows the project's conventions and holds, in 150 to 250 words of prose:

- two to four sentences on what goes wrong, and under which of the report's `conditions`;
- the minimal reproducer inline, and a few lines of its real output;
- the exact versions it was run on, the crate's, the C library's and the toolchain's; and
- one or two sentences on a possible fix.

Every statement in it is one the review verified by running or reading: no history, no
counts, no comparison with other projects and no speculation about exploitability. It
uses none of the campaign's vocabulary, such as a wave, a batch or an objective. It ends
with: `Found by [Crustify](https://github.com/crustify-rs/crustify), an experimental
UB/soundness auditing agent developed at UC Berkeley and running on <model name>, then
manually reviewed and independently reproduced.`

A possible fix may be tried on a copy of the tree in the batch's scratch, without `fix`:
the draft calls it tested only when the reproducer stops failing and the crate's own
tests pass with it. A patch is offered only under `fix`.

/*

 *
 * This file is part of libgit2, distributed under the GNU GPL v2 with
 * a Linking Exception. For full terms see the included COPYING file.
 */
#ifndef INCLUDE_ctype_compat_h__
#define INCLUDE_ctype_compat_h__

/*
 * The Microsoft C runtime (MSVCRT) may take a heavy lock on the
 * locale in order to figure out how the `ctype` functions work.
 * This is deeply slow. Provide our own to avoid that.
 */

#ifdef GIT_WIN32

GIT_INLINE(int) git__tolower(int c)
{
	return (c >= 'A' && c <= 'Z') ? (c + 32) : c;
}

GIT_INLINE(int) git__toupper(int c)
{
	return (c >= 'a' && c <= 'z') ? (c - 32) : c;
}

GIT_INLINE(bool) git__isalpha(int c)
{
	return ((c >= 'A' && c <= 'Z') || (c >= 'a' && c <= 'z'));
}

GIT_INLINE(bool) git__isdigit(int c)
{
	return (c >= '0' && c <= '9');
}

GIT_INLINE(bool) git__isalnum(int c)
{
	return git__isalpha(c) || git__isdigit(c);
}

GIT_INLINE(bool) git__isspace(int c)
{
	return (c == ' ' || c == '\t' || c == '\n' || c == '\f' || c == '\r' || c == '\v');
}

GIT_INLINE(bool) git__isxdigit(int c)
{
	return ((c >= '0' && c <= '9') || (c >= 'a' && c <= 'f') || (c >= 'A' && c <= 'F'));
}

GIT_INLINE(bool) git__isprint(int c)
{
	return (c >= ' ' && c <= '~');
}

#else
# define git__tolower(a) tolower((unsigned char)(a))
# define git__toupper(a) toupper((unsigned char)(a))

# define git__isalpha(a)  (!!isalpha((unsigned char)(a)))
# define git__isdigit(a)  (!!isdigit((unsigned char)(a)))
# define git__isalnum(a)  (!!isalnum((unsigned char)(a)))
# define git__isspace(a)  (!!isspace((unsigned char)(a)))
# define git__isxdigit(a) (!!isxdigit((unsigned char)(a)))
# define git__isprint(a)  (!!isprint((unsigned char)(a)))
#endif

#endif

#ifndef INCLUDE_ctype_compat_h__
#define INCLUDE_ctype_compat_h__

/*
 * The Microsoft C runtime (MSVCRT) may take a heavy lock on the
 * locale in order to figure out how the `ctype` functions work.
 * This is deeply slow. Provide our own to avoid that.
 */

#ifdef GIT_WIN32

GIT_INLINE(int) git__tolower(int c)
{
	return (c >= 'A' && c <= 'Z') ? (c + 32) : c;
}

GIT_INLINE(int) git__toupper(int c)
{
	return (c >= 'a' && c <= 'z') ? (c - 32) : c;
}

GIT_INLINE(bool) git__isalpha(int c)
{
	return ((c >= 'A' && c <= 'Z') || (c >= 'a' && c <= 'z'));
}

GIT_INLINE(bool) git__isdigit(int c)
{
	return (c >= '0' && c <= '9');
}

GIT_INLINE(bool) git__isalnum(int c)
{
	return git__isalpha(c) || git__isdigit(c);
}

GIT_INLINE(bool) git__isspace(int c)
{
	return (c == ' ' || c == '\t' || c == '\n' || c == '\f' || c == '\r' || c == '\v');
}

GIT_INLINE(bool) git__isxdigit(int c)
{
	return ((c >= '0' && c <= '9') || (c >= 'a' && c <= 'f') || (c >= 'A' && c <= 'F'));
}

GIT_INLINE(bool) git__isprint(int c)
{
	return (c >= ' ' && c <= '~');
}

#else
# define git__tolower(a) tolower((unsigned char)(a))
# define git__toupper(a) toupper((unsigned char)(a))

# define git__isalpha(a)  (!!isalpha((unsigned char)(a)))
# define git__isdigit(a)  (!!isdigit((unsigned char)(a)))
# define git__isalnum(a)  (!!isalnum((unsigned char)(a)))
# define git__isspace(a)  (!!isspace((unsigned char)(a)))
# define git__isxdigit(a) (!!isxdigit((unsigned char)(a)))
# define git__isprint(a)  (!!isprint((unsigned char)(a)))
#endif

#endif

1	//! `src/util/ctype_compat.h`: the locale-independent character classes libgit2 names
     2	//! `git__is*` and `git__to*`, ported to Rust.
     3	//!
     4	//! The header has no translation unit and no state: its eight items are native Rust, reached
     5	//! by no C, so the module has no unsafe regions and no exports. The macros stay in the header
     6	//! for the C that still expands them, in 33 files of `src/` (`config.c`, `date.c`, `parse.c`,
     7	//! `str.c`, `util.c` and `trailer.c` among them) and three C tests
     8	//! (`tests/util/sortedcache.c`, `tests/libgit2/clone/local.c` and `tests/libgit2/repo/open.c`),
     9	//! where they name libc's `<ctype.h>`, as porting's Macros section keeps a header's macro.
    10	//!
    11	//! # The header's branches
    12	//!
    13	//! This build is not `GIT_WIN32`, so each macro is `<ctype.h>`'s function over its argument
    14	//! cast to `unsigned char`, its predicates normalised to `0` or `1` by `!!`:
    15	//! `#define git__isalpha(a) (!!isalpha((unsigned char)(a)))`. Under `GIT_WIN32`, where the C
    16	//! runtime takes a lock on the locale in each call, the header defines them instead as
    17	//! `GIT_INLINE` functions that compare their `int` with ASCII ranges.
    18	//!

    20	//! return for it: a C caller's `git__isspace(c)` is `is_space(c as u8)`, the cast its own.
    21	//! For every byte, the `GIT_WIN32` comparisons and `<ctype.h>` in the C locale, which libgit2
    22	//! never leaves, give the same result. The branches part only on what the cast hides: an
    23	//! `int` outside a byte's range, such as `EOF` or a `char` past ASCII where `char` is
    24	//! signed, which `GIT_WIN32` compares as given (`git__tolower(-1)` is `-1`) and every other
    25	//! build reduces to its byte first (`255`), and a process locale that a program embedding
    26	//! libgit2 sets with `setlocale`, which `<ctype.h>` follows, and these functions do not.

    28	//! no byte past ASCII is a character there; a single-byte locale, as `ISO-8859-1`'s, may
    29	//! class some of those bytes as letters, and map their case.

    91	#[must_use]

    95	}

   113	#[inline]

   127	///

   129	/// assert!(!is_space(b'\0') && !is_space(0x85) && !is_space(0xA0));
   130	/// ```
   131	///

   133	#[doc(alias = "git__isspace")]
   134	#[must_use]
   135	#[inline]
   136	pub const fn is_space(c: u8) -> bool {
   137	    c == 0x0B || c.is_ascii_whitespace()
   138	}
   139

   141	///
   142	/// C's `git__isxdigit(c)` is `!!isxdigit((unsigned char)(c))`: this is its result for that
   143	/// byte, as the module's documentation describes.
   144	///
   145	/// ```
   146	/// use libgit2_crustify::libgit2::src::util::ctype_compat_h::is_xdigit;
   147	///
   148	/// assert!(is_xdigit(b'0') && is_xdigit(b'f') && is_xdigit(b'F'));
   149	/// assert!(!is_xdigit(b'g') && !is_xdigit(b'G') && !is_xdigit(b'x'));
   150	/// ```
   151	///
   152	/// Replaces `mac::git__isxdigit`
   153	#[doc(alias = "git__isxdigit")]
   154	#[must_use]
   155	#[inline]
   156	pub const fn is_xdigit(c: u8) -> bool {
   157	    c.is_ascii_hexdigit()
   158	}
   159

   161	/// byte is returned unchanged.
   162	///

   173	/// ```
   174	///

   176	#[doc(alias = "git__tolower")]
   177	#[must_use]
   178	#[inline]
   179	pub const fn to_lower(c: u8) -> u8 {

   181	}

   184	/// byte is returned unchanged.

   191	///
   192	/// assert_eq!(to_upper(b'a'), b'A');
   193	/// assert_eq!(to_upper(b'Z'), b'Z');
   194	/// assert_eq!(to_upper(b'`'), b'`');
   195	/// assert_eq!(to_upper(0xE9), 0xE9);
   196	/// ```
   197	///
   198	/// Replaces `mac::git__toupper`
   199	#[doc(alias = "git__toupper")]
   200	#[must_use]
   201	#[inline]
   202	pub const fn to_upper(c: u8) -> u8 {
   203	    c.to_ascii_uppercase()
   204	}

# A macro's configured branches are compared over the arguments its Rust form takes

Status: `open`.

Goal: Idiomatic Rust, and Least constraint: the shim the rule keeps for branches that differ
would bind libc where the Rust form can state the one result its callers receive.

## Signal

A landed row's recurrence signal: `config-branches-of-one-result` (crustify `769d102`),
"a task message or plan correction that settles again whether a configuration-dependent
macro is ported or shimmed". `wave-220/batch-0/run-1`'s task message settled it again:
"Where the header has several configured branches, port what this build defines, as
`porting-symbols`' Macros section and `strnlen_h.rs` do."

## Evidence

`wave-220/batch-0/run-1` ported `src/util/ctype_compat.h`'s eight macros, `git__isalnum`,
`git__isalpha`, `git__isdigit`, `git__isprint`, `git__isspace`, `git__isxdigit`,
`git__tolower` and `git__toupper`. The header has two branches:

- this build's: `# define git__tolower(a) tolower((unsigned char)(a))`, and
  `(!!isalpha((unsigned char)(a)))` for each class, libc's `<ctype.h>`; and
- `GIT_WIN32`'s: `GIT_INLINE` functions comparing the `int` with ASCII ranges,
  `return (c >= 'A' && c <= 'Z') ? (c + 32) : c;`.

`porting-symbols`' Macros section ports such a macro once "where every configuration's
expansion computes the same result for every input", and keeps the shim for one "whose
branches differ in what they compute". Read over the C's inputs, the `int` each macro
takes, these branches differ: `git__tolower(-1)` is `-1` under `GIT_WIN32` and `255`
elsewhere, `git__tolower(0x141)` is `0x141` and `'a'`. Read over the byte the expansion's own
cast leaves, the argument every other build classes, they agree for each of the 256: the
run checked it in glibc's `C`, `POSIX` and `C.UTF-8` locales against the `GIT_WIN32`
comparisons (`branches.c` beside this proposal, run as `cc branches.c && ./a.out <locale>`: 0 bytes differing in each),
and the batch's equivalence tests compare the ports with glibc's functions for every `int`
from -300 to 600. The Rust form takes that byte, a `u8`, and its C callers' cast is
written where they call it, `c as u8`. Which reading the rule means, the rule does not say,
so the task message had to.

The process locale, which `<ctype.h>` reads and the Rust does not, is a second difference the
rule's "configuration" leaves open: it is no build configuration, but the state of an
out-of-tree library's entity, which `dependencies.json` already records in the entity's
`match` and note ("libgit2 runs in the C locale, where glibc's tables agree") and which its
route's confirmation checks.

## Destination

The spec: `porting-symbols`' Macros section.

## Change

In its second paragraph, replace "is ported once where every configuration's expansion
computes the same result for every input, and its documentation names the branches the
build does not take" with:

> is ported once where every configuration's expansion computes the same result for every
> input its Rust form takes: the arguments the expansion's own conversions leave, such as a
> cast to `unsigned char`, which its Rust callers make where they call it. Its documentation
> names the branches the build does not take, and the arguments outside that domain on
> which they part. The runtime state an out-of-tree entity of the expansion reads, such as
> the locale `<ctype.h>` follows, is no configuration: the entity's route and its
> confirmation settle it, as `dependencies`' Confirmation section describes.

## Validation

`wave-220/batch-0`'s port and tests, as the evidence describes: 11 `unit_pub` tests check
every byte against the C standard's C-locale classes, and 5 `equiv` tests compare the ports
with glibc's `<ctype.h>` for every `int` in -300..=600 and through three of the C's
expansion sites. A mutant `is_space` without the vertical tab fails three of them.

## Record

The row for `EVOLUTION.md`, copied in when the change lands:

| change | from | landed as | signal answered | recurrence signal | status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| a configuration-dependent macro's branches are compared over the arguments its Rust form takes, after the expansion's own conversions; an out-of-tree entity's runtime state, such as the locale, is its route's, not a configuration | `libgit2-crustify`, `config-branches-over-the-rust-domain` | — | `config-branches-of-one-result`'s recurrence: a task message settled again whether `ctype_compat.h`'s macros, whose branches part only on `int`s outside a byte, are ported or shimmed | a task message or plan correction that settles again whether a configuration-dependent macro is ported or shimmed, or a review finding of a shim over branches that agree on the Rust form's domain | — |

## Review

None yet.
/* Compares <ctype.h> in the locale argv[1] names with ctype_compat.h's GIT_WIN32 branch, for every byte. */
#include <ctype.h>
#include <locale.h>
#include <stdio.h>
int main(int argc, char **argv) {
  if (!setlocale(LC_ALL, argv[1])) { printf("no locale %s\n", argv[1]); return 1; }
  int diff = 0;
  for (int c = 0; c < 256; c++) {
    int a = !!isalpha(c), d = !!isdigit(c), n = !!isalnum(c), p = !!isprint(c), s = !!isspace(c), x = !!isxdigit(c);
    int ea = (c>='A'&&c<='Z')||(c>='a'&&c<='z'), ed = c>='0'&&c<='9', es = c==' '||c=='\t'||c=='\n'||c=='\f'||c=='\r'||c=='\v';
    int ex = ed||(c>='a'&&c<='f')||(c>='A'&&c<='F'), ep = c>=' '&&c<='~';
    int el = (c>='A'&&c<='Z')?c+32:c, eu = (c>='a'&&c<='z')?c-32:c;
    if (a!=ea||d!=ed||n!=(ea||ed)||p!=ep||s!=es||x!=ex||tolower(c)!=el||toupper(c)!=eu) { diff++; printf("%s differs at %d\n", argv[1], c); }
  }
  printf("%s: %d bytes differ from GIT_WIN32's comparisons\n", argv[1], diff);
  return 0;
}

content.content:
---
name: evolution
description: "How Crustify repairs and improves itself from what its campaigns expose: goals, signals, proposals, lessons, evolution branches, validation, review, autonomy, adoption, and where the record of what landed is kept. Read before filing a defect in Crustify or a tool, proposing or making a change to either, or recording a campaign's lesson; `evolution-record` holds the record and how evolution itself evolves."
---

# Evolution

How a campaign changes the harness that runs it, Crustify's skills, agents, templates and
providers, its tools and the tools it lacks, and how its agents propose changes to the
campaign's artifacts that other roles own. A campaign exposes what the harness gets
wrong, what it constrains needlessly and what it repeats by hand; evolution turns that
evidence into changes, under the autonomy the settings' `evolution` answer grants, and
this guidance itself among them. Where a change goes within Crustify is
[`authoring`](../authoring/SKILL.md)'s.

## 1. Goals

Every change is judged against Crustify's goals, [`GOALS.md`](../../../GOALS.md), read in
full before the first proposal: a change serves one of them, or it is not made. The goals
are evolved too, when the evidence questions them, as `GOALS.md` describes.

A change to a tool is judged against that tool's own goals and non-goals too, the document
its tool skill names, read in full before the first change to the tool: they keep what the
tool is from drifting, such as an analysis that stays syntactic and does no data-flow
analysis. A change that departs from one of them is proposed, not made, and says so. A
tool with no such document has every change that alters what it is, rather than fixing or
extending what it does, proposed, not made.
<!-- TODO: ffimap has no goals document yet. -->

## 2. Signals

Evolution starts from evidence a campaign produces, never from taste:

| signal | what it suggests |
|---|---|
| a tool that crashes, or reports what the source contradicts | a defect in the tool |
| skills that contradict each other, or an agent prompt that leads its agent wrong | a defect in the spec |
| a rule an agent works around, or that forces a worse result than its omission would | an overconstraining rule, loosened or removed |
| review findings that recur across batches, in one objective or category | a rule the how-to skills lack |
| failed or rerun batches, and plan corrections | a defect in planning, scheduling or packing |
| the user's corrections | a rule, or a lesson of the campaign |
| cost or time outliers, in the dashboard | waste in batch sizing, gates or tooling |
| one representation hand-written in several places, or a TODO met again and again | a primitive or tool feature that is missing |
| one procedure repeated by hand: the same script written again, the same queries run in sequence | a tool, or a subcommand of one |
| a signal evolution missed, or a proposal that proved wrong | a defect in this guidance |
| a goal no decision cites, two that keep conflicting the same way, or a well-founded change no goal serves | a change to the goals |

A proposal needs one of these, with its evidence: a defect, a failure, a recurring
finding, a workaround or a measured waste. Fewer, well-founded proposals serve better than
many small ones: a change made for style alone, or for completeness, or to have proposed
something, is not made.

## 3. Destinations

Each signal goes to one destination:

- **the campaign alone**: what a setting or a task message settles, which changes nothing
  of Crustify;
- **a lesson**: a rule that holds for this target alone, recorded in the campaign's
  [`LESSONS.md`](#5-lessons);
- **the spec**: a skill, an agent, a template or a provider, where `authoring` places it;
- **a tool**: its code, its documentation or its tests, or a new tool; or
- **a campaign artifact**: the plan, the dependencies, the schedule or the dashboard, where
  the evidence shows one wrong or improvable and another role owns it. Its owner applies
  the proposal or declines it, a plan's at the next planner run.

A rule an agent cannot follow because its host refuses it, a write or a tool call
blocked, or a launch mode that withholds what the role needs, is a defect of that host's
provider, not of the rule: the provider prevents it with whatever its host offers, its
agents' definitions, the settings and permissions it installs, its hooks, the mode it
launches runs in, or the host's memory, and the spec is not bent around one host. Until
the provider's change lands, a run that meets the refusal neither works around it nor drops
what it could not do: it hands that to the assistant, in its final message, and the
assistant carries it out.

The test between a lesson and the spec is generality: a rule that can only be stated in
the target's own names is a lesson, and one the spec takes is stated without them, as it
would hold for any C codebase.

## 4. Proposals

A proposal is filed in the campaign's repository under `crustify/evolution/<slug>/`, as its
`PROPOSAL.md`. It states:

- the signal and its evidence, with the runs, findings and commits it cites;
- the goal it serves, by name, and the fitness measure of that goal it expects to move;
- its destination;
- the change, or the patch;
- how it was validated;
- the row the record takes when the change lands, as [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md) describes;
- its review's verdict; and

## 1. Goals

Every change is judged against Crustify's goals, [`GOALS.md`](../../../GOALS.md), read in
full before the first proposal: a change serves one of them, or it is not made. The goals
are evolved too, when the evidence questions them, as `GOALS.md` describes.

A change to a tool is judged against that tool's own goals and non-goals too, the document
its tool skill names, read in full before the first change to the tool: they keep what the
tool is from drifting, such as an analysis that stays syntactic and does no data-flow
analysis. A change that departs from one of them is proposed, not made, and says so. A
tool with no such document has every change that alters what it is, rather than fixing or
extending what it does, proposed, not made.

put to the user at the next module's end. A change to a protected text always waits for the
user. A
change to `GOALS.md` is proposed and never made, unless the user asks for it, since
`GOALS.md` is what every other change is judged against.

A component's `devel` is the user's gate. It takes a campaign's working branch only with
the user's approval, asked for at each module's end and at the campaign's end, with the
record's entries since the last advance, those the review marked as weakening a check
first. Where `devel` has moved meanwhile, the working branch takes it by merge before it
is offered. What the user declines is reverted on the working branch or stays there, as
they say, and is recorded so; where it weakened a check, what landed under it is reviewed
again, by review batches with `revisit`, as [Adoption](#10-adoption) schedules them for a
soundness fix. Merging a component's `devel` into its `main`, and merging a
new tool upstream, need the user's approval too.

A run that a defect blocks does not work around it. Where the answer lets fixes land, it
makes the fix on its evolution branch; under `propose` it files the proposal, with its
reproducer, and the user is asked at once whether the fix is to be made; and it ends,
reporting which. The fix is reviewed and lands, and the run is run again, as a failed
batch is.

## 10. Adoption

Every run's `task.json` records the revisions of Crustify and the tools it launched
under, as [`task-schema`](../../artifacts/task-schema/SKILL.md)'s Run fields section
describes. A change that lands on a working branch takes effect as it lands: the runs launched
after it record its revision, and a run under way when it lands, which its recorded
revisions and its landing's date tell, may have followed either. What landed before it
under the old rules stays, unless the change fixes a soundness
defect: then the landings it affects are reviewed again, by a review batch with
`revisit`.

At each module's end, the campaign's evolution is consolidated: open proposals are landed
as the autonomy allows, the working branches are offered to the user for `devel`, and the
revisit batches a soundness fix or a declined weakening calls for are scheduled. The
lessons are reconciled when [Lessons](#5-lessons) times it, and the record's rows are read
when [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md) times it.

## 11. The record

The record of what landed, `EVOLUTION.md`, and how evolution itself evolves from it are
[`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md)'s.

9. **Should review batches be capped? They are packed larger than translation batches,
   since a reviewer reads landed code rather than writing it.** (`id: review-workload`)
   - Answer: `assistant's choice`

10. **Which objectives should review agents review for? By default, every one the
    reviewer offers.** (`id: review-objectives`)
    - Answer: `all`
    - Without `fix`, reviewers report and reproduce what they find but patch nothing.

11. **Which sanitizers should the campaign build and test under? By default, every one
    the toolchain supports.** (`id: sanitizers`)
    - Answer: `asan-ubsan, tsan, bsan`, the variants `crustify/artifacts/build.json`
      records; MSan is not built.
    - From 2026-11-14 BSan runs as the `testing-gates` skill's Regressions section has it,
      with no departure: for a batch, on the tests its own work adds or changes, each named
      and alone; at a wave's and a module's end, over the workspace less the slow list,
      `crustify/scripts/slow-list.txt`; and whole in each full run. The departure of
      2026-11-13, BSan over the workspace only before a ship point, ended when that rule
      landed.
    - Miri needs no build and is always on.

12. **How should the target be configured: which of its build features should be
    enabled or disabled?** (`id: target-config`)
    - Answer: the configuration `crustify/artifacts/build.json` records: deprecated
      features disabled (`-DDEPRECATE_HARD=ON`), HTTPS through OpenSSL, SSH, Negotiate
      auth and i18n off, threads on.

13. **At which points should the hybrid C-Rust program ship? Shipping advances `main` to
    what the campaign has integrated, with your approval each time: the modules shipped
    are translated, and the C still left is reached only through the wrappers on its
    boundary.** (`id: ship`)
    - Answer: `after:` `src/libgit2/repository.c` and every module its `schedule.json`
      record reaches through `depends_on.scheduled`, 42 modules of about 15.8K lines of C,
      their `wrap` and `port` waves planned through wave 781: `src/libgit2/buf.c`,
      `src/libgit2/common.h`, `src/libgit2/config.c`, `src/libgit2/grafts.c`,
      `src/libgit2/object.c`, `src/libgit2/odb.c`, `src/libgit2/oid.c`,
      `src/libgit2/oidarray.c`, `src/libgit2/parse.c`, `src/libgit2/refs.c`,
      `src/libgit2/repository.c`, `src/libgit2/strarray.c`, `src/libgit2/sysdir.c`,
      `src/util/alloc.c`, `src/util/allocators/failalloc.c`, `src/util/array.h`,
      `src/util/cc-compat.h`, `src/util/ctype_compat.h`, `src/util/errors.c`,
      `src/util/filebuf.c`, `src/util/fs_path.c`, `src/util/futils.c`, `src/util/hash.c`,
      `src/util/hash/collisiondetect.c`, `src/util/hash/openssl.c`,
      `src/util/hash/sha1dc/sha1.c`, `src/util/hash/sha1dc/ubc_check.c`,
      `src/util/hashmap.h`, `src/util/hashmap_str.h`, `src/util/integer.h`,
      `src/util/pool.c`, `src/util/posix.c`, `src/util/rand.c`, `src/util/regexp.c`,
      `src/util/runtime.c`, `src/util/str.c`, `src/util/thread.c`, `src/util/tsort.c`,
      `src/util/unix/map.c`, `src/util/unix/realpath.c`, `src/util/util.c`,
      `src/util/vector.c`: the first ship point, chosen by the user on 2026-11-15 in place
      of the list by size (about 15K lines of integrated leaves, through wave 338). A
      re-plan that changes the closure changes this list with it. `src/util/alloc.c` and
      `src/util/allocators/failalloc.c` are wrapped, not ported, and the dependencies the
      order cuts stay C behind wrappers at this point. Later points are core modules
      with their closures too, each confirmed with the user; `src/libgit2/commit.c`, nine
      modules further, is the candidate for the second.
    - `decide after planning`: once the plan is complete, I propose ship points from it,
      with the boundary each would leave, and record your choice here.
    - By default: after every integrated module.

## Evolution

14. **How far may the campaign evolve Crustify and its tools from what it exposes? Agents
    file proposals and record the target's lessons; fixes and improvements land, once
    another agent has reviewed them, on a working branch of each component that is the
    campaign's own, and reach the component's `devel` only with your approval.**
    (`id: evolution`)
    - Answer: `evolve`, on the campaign's working branches (`libgit2-crustify/devel` of each
      component, checked out since 2026-11-14 in a worktree of its own beside the
      component's checkout, `/crustify-rs/<component>.libgit2-crustify`, the component's
      own checkout being on `devel`; a session of this campaign loads Crustify from that
      worktree, `--plugin-dir /crustify-rs/crustify.libgit2-crustify`): a change lands
      there once its review approves it, and each component's `devel` takes the working
      branch only with the user's approval, as crustify `c2f21a0`'s model has it. The
      former `unattended: the whole campaign` is retired with it.
    - `propose`: proposals and lessons only. `repair`: also fixes of defects. `evolve`: also
      improvements and new tools. You are asked to take the working branches into `devel`
      at each module's end and the campaign's end.

## Commits

15. **Which git identity should the campaign's commits carry: an author, and any
    co-authors? By default, Crustify's own, `crustify <crustify@berkeley.edu>` (the
    GitHub account `crustify-ai`), as the author, with no co-author.** (`id: identity`)
    - Answer: `author: Marius Momeu <marius.momeu@berkeley.edu>, co-authors: crustify
      <crustify@berkeley.edu>` (the GitHub account `crustify-ai`)

## Autonomy (if question 6 is answered `no`)

Answer these approval-gate questions only if question 6 is answered `no`.

    - Answer: `no`

    (`id: gates.translation`)
    - Answer: `no`
18. **Should I wait for your approval before integrating each module into the working
    branch?** (`id: gates.module`)
    - Answer: `no`
19. **Should I wait for your approval before starting review passes?** (`id: gates.review`)
    - Answer: `no`

#!/bin/bash
# Run cargo against one crustify prebuild of libgit2, instrumenting Rust to match.
#
#   crustify/scripts/cargo-variant.sh <variant> <cargo subcommand> [args...]
#
# <variant> is a `variants` key of crustify/artifacts/build.json: plain, coverage, asan-ubsan,
# tsan or bsan. Each variant uses its own target dir under target/.
# The safe crate's build script, in campaign mode, links the variant's static archive (its
# `static` in build.json) into each test binary, so the C runs under the instrumentation the
# Rust is built with here, one runtime serving both. Set CRUSTIFY_BUILD_DIR to a private build
# of the variant, which carries the same archive, to link it instead of the shared one.
set -euo pipefail
variant=${1:?usage: cargo-variant.sh <variant> <cargo subcommand> [args...]}
shift
here=$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/../.." && pwd)
host=x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
export CRUSTIFY_BUILD_VARIANT=$variant
export CARGO_TARGET_DIR=${CARGO_TARGET_DIR:-$here/target/$variant}
# pcre2-sys links the variant's side-campaign PCRE2, the one libgit2's C links, rather than
# building its vendored copy, which would shadow it in every test binary. The side campaigns'
# clones sit where the variant's build found their installs, beside the repository whose
# crustify/builds holds it (build.json's configure takes them from `$PWD/../../../..` in
# crustify/builds/<variant>): resolved physically through crustify/builds, which a worktree or
# a gate snapshot links to that repository's, so that every checkout finds the same ones.
side=$(realpath -m "$here/crustify/builds/$variant/../../../..")
export PKG_CONFIG_PATH="$side/pcre2-bindings/crustify/builds/$variant/install/lib/pkgconfig${PKG_CONFIG_PATH:+:$PKG_CONFIG_PATH}"
cd "$here"
# The nightly the workspace pins, for the sanitizers that need it.
nightly=$(sed -n 's/^nightly = "\(.*\)"$/\1/p' Cargo.toml)
# Cargo's own flags must come before a `--`, which hands the rest to the test binaries.
pre=() post=()
for arg in "$@"; do
  if [ ${#post[@]} -gt 0 ] || [ "$arg" = -- ]; then post+=("$arg"); else pre+=("$arg"); fi
done
case $variant in
  plain)
    exec cargo "$@" ;;
  coverage)
    # Source-based coverage on the pinned nightly, against the variant's clang-instrumented C,
    # which each test binary links statically, so that rustc's profiler runtime counts both;
    # crustify/scripts/coverage/ measures the suites as the testing spec's Coverage section does.
    export RUSTFLAGS="${RUSTFLAGS:-} -C instrument-coverage"
    export RUSTDOCFLAGS="${RUSTDOCFLAGS:-} -C instrument-coverage"
    export LLVM_PROFILE_FILE=${LLVM_PROFILE_FILE:-$CARGO_TARGET_DIR/profraw/%p-%m.profraw}
    exec cargo "+$nightly" "${pre[@]}" --target $host "${post[@]}" ;;
  asan-ubsan)
    export RUSTFLAGS="${RUSTFLAGS:-} -Zsanitizer=address -Cforce-frame-pointers=yes"
    export RUSTDOCFLAGS="${RUSTDOCFLAGS:-} -Zsanitizer=address"
    export ASAN_OPTIONS=${ASAN_OPTIONS:-detect_leaks=1:abort_on_error=1}
    export UBSAN_OPTIONS=${UBSAN_OPTIONS:-print_stacktrace=1:halt_on_error=1}
    exec cargo "+$nightly" "${pre[@]}" --target $host "${post[@]}" ;;
  tsan)
    export RUSTFLAGS="${RUSTFLAGS:-} -Zsanitizer=thread"
    export RUSTDOCFLAGS="${RUSTDOCFLAGS:-} -Zsanitizer=thread"
    # glibc's tzset locks what TSan cannot see: see tsan.supp.
    export TSAN_OPTIONS=${TSAN_OPTIONS:-halt_on_error=1:suppressions=$here/crustify/scripts/tsan.supp}
    exec cargo "+$nightly" "${pre[@]}" -Zbuild-std --target $host "${post[@]}" ;;
  bsan)
    # trybuild's nested cargo build does not finish under BorrowSanitizer, and the
    # compile-fail suite is a compile-time check the plain variant already runs.

#!/bin/bash
# Run cargo against one crustify prebuild of libgit2, instrumenting Rust to match.
#
#   crustify/scripts/cargo-variant.sh <variant> <cargo subcommand> [args...]
#
# <variant> is a `variants` key of crustify/artifacts/build.json: plain, coverage, asan-ubsan,
# tsan or bsan. Each variant uses its own target dir under target/.
# The safe crate's build script, in campaign mode, links the variant's static archive (its
# `static` in build.json) into each test binary, so the C runs under the instrumentation the
# Rust is built with here, one runtime serving both. Set CRUSTIFY_BUILD_DIR to a private build
# of the variant, which carries the same archive, to link it instead of the shared one.
set -euo pipefail
variant=${1:?usage: cargo-variant.sh <variant> <cargo subcommand> [args...]}
shift
here=$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/../.." && pwd)
host=x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
export CRUSTIFY_BUILD_VARIANT=$variant
export CARGO_TARGET_DIR=${CARGO_TARGET_DIR:-$here/target/$variant}
# pcre2-sys links the variant's side-campaign PCRE2, the one libgit2's C links, rather than
# building its vendored copy, which would shadow it in every test binary. The side campaigns'
# clones sit where the variant's build found their installs, beside the repository whose
# crustify/builds holds it (build.json's configure takes them from `$PWD/../../../..` in
# crustify/builds/<variant>): resolved physically through crustify/builds, which a worktree or
# a gate snapshot links to that repository's, so that every checkout finds the same ones.
side=$(realpath -m "$here/crustify/builds/$variant/../../../..")
export PKG_CONFIG_PATH="$side/pcre2-bindings/crustify/builds/$variant/install/lib/pkgconfig${PKG_CONFIG_PATH:+:$PKG_CONFIG_PATH}"
cd "$here"
# The nightly the workspace pins, for the sanitizers that need it.
nightly=$(sed -n 's/^nightly = "\(.*\)"$/\1/p' Cargo.toml)
# Cargo's own flags must come before a `--`, which hands the rest to the test binaries.
pre=() post=()
for arg in "$@"; do
  if [ ${#post[@]} -gt 0 ] || [ "$arg" = -- ]; then post+=("$arg"); else pre+=("$arg"); fi
done
case $variant in
  plain)
    exec cargo "$@" ;;
  coverage)
    # Source-based coverage on the pinned nightly, against the variant's clang-instrumented C,
    # which each test binary links statically, so that rustc's profiler runtime counts both;
    # crustify/scripts/coverage/ measures the suites as the testing spec's Coverage section does.
    export RUSTFLAGS="${RUSTFLAGS:-} -C instrument-coverage"
    export RUSTDOCFLAGS="${RUSTDOCFLAGS:-} -C instrument-coverage"
    export LLVM_PROFILE_FILE=${LLVM_PROFILE_FILE:-$CARGO_TARGET_DIR/profraw/%p-%m.profraw}
    exec cargo "+$nightly" "${pre[@]}" --target $host "${post[@]}" ;;
  asan-ubsan)
    export RUSTFLAGS="${RUSTFLAGS:-} -Zsanitizer=address -Cforce-frame-pointers=yes"
    export RUSTDOCFLAGS="${RUSTDOCFLAGS:-} -Zsanitizer=address"
    export ASAN_OPTIONS=${ASAN_OPTIONS:-detect_leaks=1:abort_on_error=1}
    export UBSAN_OPTIONS=${UBSAN_OPTIONS:-print_stacktrace=1:halt_on_error=1}
    exec cargo "+$nightly" "${pre[@]}" --target $host "${post[@]}" ;;
  tsan)
    export RUSTFLAGS="${RUSTFLAGS:-} -Zsanitizer=thread"
    export RUSTDOCFLAGS="${RUSTDOCFLAGS:-} -Zsanitizer=thread"
    # glibc's tzset locks what TSan cannot see: see tsan.supp.
    export TSAN_OPTIONS=${TSAN_OPTIONS:-halt_on_error=1:suppressions=$here/crustify/scripts/tsan.supp}
    exec cargo "+$nightly" "${pre[@]}" -Zbuild-std --target $host "${post[@]}" ;;
  bsan)
    # trybuild's nested cargo build does not finish under BorrowSanitizer, and the
    # compile-fail suite is a compile-time check the plain variant already runs.

[package]
name = "libgit2-crustify"
description = "Safe Rust wrappers over libgit2's public API."
edition.workspace = true
rust-version.workspace = true
version.workspace = true
license.workspace = true
repository.workspace = true
publish.workspace = true
# The raw bindings' link metadata, which dependents' build scripts read as `DEP_GIT2_*`.
links = "git2"
build = "build.rs"
# The packaged crate: the safe crate, its raw bindings and the C its bundled build reads
# (crustify's `bindgen` skill, Publishing).
include = [
    "/Cargo.toml",
    "/build.rs",
    "/build/**",
    "/README.md",
    "/src/**",
    "/sys/**",
    "/c/COPYING",
    "/c/CMakeLists.txt",
    "/c/cmake/**",
    "/c/include/**",
    "/c/src/CMakeLists.txt",
    "/c/src/cli/**",
    "/c/src/libgit2/**",
    "/c/src/util/**",
    "/c/deps/llhttp/**",
    "/c/deps/ntlmclient/**",
    "/c/deps/reftable/**",
    "/c/deps/xdiff/**",
]

[features]
# Every link unit, so that the campaign's builds, lints and tests, which take the default
# features, cover each one the campaign ports.
default = ["libgit2", "git2"]
# One feature per link unit; each gates its module in src/lib.rs, and src/sys.rs's when the
# link unit is optional.
libgit2 = []
# The CLI (src/cli), whose C links libgit2's: the bundled build compiles its objects, and
# the `shared` and `system` modes, whose libraries hold none, refuse it.
git2 = ["libgit2"]
# Regenerates the raw bindings into OUT_DIR from the headers of the C a build links, in
# place of the committed ones; campaign mode checks them against the committed ones
# (crustify's `bindgen` skill, Build modes).
bindgen = ["dep:bindgen"]
# Builds `c/` as shared libraries in place of static ones.
shared = []
# Links an install of libgit2, found through LIBGIT2_DIR or pkg-config, in place of `c/`.
system = []
# The export features: one per ported module not yet switched from C, which compiles its
# `ffi_export` gateway, the bare-named exports through which the remaining C calls it. Each
# stays off until its module switches, so that the exports never collide with the C they
# replace, and the switch deletes it (crustify's conventions, Export features). None is
# declared while every ported module has switched: those of `src/util/utf8.c`,
# `src/cli/opt.c`, `deps/llhttp/api.c` and `deps/llhttp/http.c` went at their switches.

[dependencies]
# By path, not by Git: trybuild replaces only the paths of dependencies declared by path
# with `$FFIBOX` in compile-fail snapshots. By the canonical path of the campaign's own
# checkout of ffibox, the worktree of its working branch, `libgit2-crustify/devel`, so that
# the crate builds against the ffibox the campaign has changed, not against `devel`'s, which
# /crustify-rs/ffibox and the /opt/venv/share/ffibox link hold. Canonical, since trybuild
# replaces the canonicalized path while rustc prints the path as declared: a path through a
# link leaves the snapshots' paths absolute. glibc-bindings takes it by Git, which the [patch] below points at this path,
# so the graph holds one ffibox.
ffibox = { version = "0.1.1", path = "/crustify-rs/ffibox.libgit2-crustify" }
# libc's wrapper, the crustify-rs/glibc-crustify side campaign: pinned to a commit
# (`wrapper.pin` in crustify/artifacts/dependencies.json), and patched below to its clone
# beside this repository while the campaign extends it, by absolute path, which the batch
# worktrees under crustify/.worktrees resolve too.
glibc-bindings = { version = "0.1.0", git = "https://github.com/crustify-rs/glibc-crustify", rev = "24da93fc31a1788e73443cf4333d5037435d2d3f" }
pcre2-sys = "0.2"
nix = { version = "0.31.3", features = ["fs", "socket", "net", "poll", "process", "user", "feature", "signal", "mman", "time", "uio", "dir", "hostname"] }
flate2 = "1.1.11"
sha2 = "0.11.1"
hmac = "0.13.0"
equiv

support
ub_safe
ub_unsafe

end-gates: run a wave's or a module's end gates over a snapshot of a tree.

    end-gates <tree> --logs <dir> [--stages lint,plain,asan-ubsan,tsan,miri,bsan]
              [--rev <rev> | --working-tree] [--package <name>] [--runner <cmd>]
              [--link <path>]... [--skip-file <file>] [--stage-env <stage>:<K>=<V>]...
              [--lint-features <features>]... [--timeout <seconds>] [--parallel <n>]
              [--nightly <toolchain>]

The gates of testing-gates' Regressions section, run exactly so:

1. The tree's commit (`--rev`, HEAD by default), or its working tree with
   `--working-tree`, is copied to a snapshot, `<tree>/crustify/tmp/gates-<label>`, so that
   work goes on in the tree while the gates run. Each submodule, and each `--link` path
   (such as the variants' builds dir), is symlinked from the tree into it, and the snapshot
   is made a git repository, since a test may discover the repository it runs in.
2. Each skip of `--skip-file` is checked against its test binary's `--list` before any
   stage runs: a skip that names no test fails the run. A run with skips passes libtest
   `--exact`, so that a skip takes its one test and no other whose name holds it. A variant
   stage's skip must also name one test of the whole workspace, since that stage runs
   every binary with the same arguments: a name another binary holds too fails the run.
3. The stages run in the order given:
   - `lint`: the workspace's format check, `cargo +<nightly> fmt --all --check`, then its
     lints with warnings denied, `<runner> plain clippy --workspace --all-targets
     [--features <features>] -- -D warnings`, once with no feature and once for each
     `--lint-features`, such as the export features of the modules not yet switched;
   - a variant (`plain` and each sanitizer but `bsan`): the workspace's tests,
     `<runner> <variant> test --workspace --no-fail-fast`, with that stage's skips;
   - `miri`: the package's test binaries built once on the pinned nightly, then one
     `cargo miri test` per test binary, side by side, each skipping `compile_fail`;
   - `bsan`: the test binaries built once, then one invocation per test binary, side by
     side, each under `--timeout`, with that stage's skips.
4. Each run writes `<logs>/<stage>[-<binary>].log`, a lint run
   `<logs>/lint-fmt.log` and `<logs>/lint-clippy[-<features>].log`; `<logs>/summary.json` and
   `summary.txt` record each run's command, exit status, duration, test-result lines and
   failed tests. A run that exceeds its timeout reports `timed_out`.

The skip file holds one skip per line, `<stage> <binary> <exact test name>`, the binary
being `lib` or an integration test's name; `#` starts a comment.

The job count is the environment's: `CARGO_BUILD_JOBS` for builds, `RUST_TEST_THREADS` for
each binary's tests, as concurrency describes. The exit status is 0 when every run
passed, 1 when any failed, and 2 when the run could not start.

Standard library only.

---
name: concurrency
description: "How much work runs at once on the host: agents in flight and each build's or test's job count. Read before launching a wave's agents or running parallel builds and gates."
---

# Concurrency

How a campaign's work shares the host it runs on: how much of it runs at once, and how
the builds, tests and gates inside it are parallelized. What runs in which order is
[scheduling](../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s; this spec describes only how much of what may run is in
flight.

## 1. Principle

Concurrency is maximized given the resources and the parallel workloads that share them,
without lengthening the latency of any unit of work. The resources are the host's cores,
memory, disk and I/O, and the providers' request rates. The parallel workloads are
everything that runs on the host at once: the campaign's agents, the agents of its side
campaigns and of other campaigns on the same host, the shared rebuilds of the target's
variants, and the gates each agent runs.

Concurrency is therefore decided when work starts, from the state of the host at that
moment, and revised as that state changes. No committed artifact fixes it.

## 2. Agents

An agent spends most of its time waiting on its model, and only part of it building and
testing. More agents can be in flight than the host has cores; what bounds them is how
much of their building and testing overlaps, the memory and disk each one's tree takes, and
the rate the provider allows.

The number of agents in flight follows from those, for each wave as it starts and again as
its batches land or fail. A `parallelism` number in the settings' `workload` answer, or an

# Concurrency

## 1. Principle

Concurrency is maximized given the resources and the parallel workloads that share them,

# `cli_opt_status_fprint`'s export writes an interrupted piece again, and reports success

- **finding**: `equiv/status-export-rewrites-an-interrupted-write`
- **batch**: `wave-186/batch-6/run-1`, the review of `git2/src/cli/opt.c`'s `symbol` route
  (batches 1, 4 and 5).
- **item**: `fn::cli_opt_status_fprint`: its export in `src/git2/src/cli/opt.rs`'s `ffi_export`,
  which writes `OptRef::write_status`'s pieces through `FileWriter`, an `io::Write` over the C
  stream (`wave-186/batch-4`, `64431c07a`).
- **affected commit**: `17401d831`, the wave's tip; since `64431c07a`.
- **class**: an equivalence defect of an export, which the CLI's remaining C (`main.c`'s and
  `opt_usage.c`'s `cli_opt_status_fprint(stderr, …)`) reaches once the module switches from C.

## Finding

C's `cli_opt_status_fprint` writes its message in a few `fprintf` calls and returns at the first
that fails. `fprintf` does not retry a write that a signal interrupts: when the `write` under it
fails with `EINTR` part way through, `fprintf` returns -1, with `errno` `EINTR`, and the bytes
that went out stay out.

The export wrote each piece with `io::Write::write_all`, which `FileWriter` did not implement: the
trait's own `write_all` calls `write` again, from the start of what is left, whenever it fails
with `io::ErrorKind::Interrupted`, the kind of `EINTR`. `FileWriter::write` was one `fprintf` of
the whole piece (`FileRef::print`), which reports an `EINTR` failure as that kind, so the piece
was written a second time, whole, after the part that had gone out, and the message went on to
its end: the export returned 0 where C returns -1, and the stream held the interrupted piece's
first bytes twice. The task's move onto `FileRef::write_all`, a `write` over it alone, keeps the
defect, since `write_all` reports `EINTR` as the same kind.

## Evidence

`src/main.rs` here compiles C's `opt.c` under other names (`build.rs`, `c_cli_opt_*`) beside the
safe crate's exports, which its export feature links in place of the variant's `opt.c`, and
calls each `cli_opt_status_fprint`, the export through its raw binding as C calls it, on a
`fopencookie` stream, unbuffered, whose first write takes three bytes and fails with `EINTR`.
From the repository root:

```text
CARGO_TARGET_DIR=crustify/tmp/target-repro crustify/scripts/cargo-variant.sh plain run -q \
  --manifest-path crustify/reviews/modules/git2/src/cli/opt.c/wave-186/batch-6/equiv/status-export-rewrites-an-interrupted-write/Cargo.toml
```

On `17401d831` it exits 1 (`run-affected.log`):

```text
C:      returned -1, errno 4, wrote "git"
export: returned 0, errno 4, wrote "gitgit2: unknown option: --nope\n"
the export departs from C
```

## Fix

`FileWriter` writes through `FileRef::write_all` (glibc-crustify `24da93f`, pinned by
`ac1f36519`), one `fwrite` of the bytes as they are, and implements `io::Write::write_all` as that
one call, so that a failure ends the message unretried, as it ends C's. Its `write`, which the
export does not call, fails whenever the `fwrite` fails, though part of the bytes may be out:
`write_all` does not report `fwrite`'s count, so no `Ok(n)` can tell how many, and the type's
documentation says so. The same change answers `crustify/evolution/fileref-prints-bytes`: the
argument, the names and the command are written as their bytes, the command through the private
`OptRef::write_status_bytes`, where the export had passed it through `to_string_lossy`.

```text
CARGO_TARGET_DIR=crustify/tmp/target-repro crustify/scripts/cargo-variant.sh plain run -q \
  --manifest-path crustify/reviews/modules/git2/src/cli/opt.c/wave-186/batch-6/equiv/status-export-rewrites-an-interrupted-write/Cargo.toml
```

On `17401d831` it exits 1 (`run-affected.log`):

```text
C:      returned -1, errno 4, wrote "git"
export: returned 0, errno 4, wrote "gitgit2: unknown option: --nope\n"
the export departs from C
```

## Fix

`FileWriter` writes through `FileRef::write_all` (glibc-crustify `24da93f`, pinned by
`ac1f36519`), one `fwrite` of the bytes as they are, and implements `io::Write::write_all` as that
one call, so that a failure ends the message unretried, as it ends C's. Its `write`, which the
export does not call, fails whenever the `fwrite` fails, though part of the bytes may be out:
`write_all` does not report `fwrite`'s count, so no `Ok(n)` can tell how many, and the type's
documentation says so. The same change answers `crustify/evolution/fileref-prints-bytes`: the
argument, the names and the command are written as their bytes, the command through the private
`OptRef::write_status_bytes`, where the export had passed it through `to_string_lossy`.
